{{Short description|Rational numbers with root 5 added}}
{{cs1 config |mode=cs1}}
{{Use dmy dates |cs1-dates=sy|date=July 2025}}

In mathematics, {{Q(√5)}},<ref>The expression {{tmath|\Q(~\!\!\sqrt5~\!)}} is pronounced "the rational numbers adjoin the square root of five", or, more concisely, "Q adjoin root five". See {{harvnb|Trifković|2013|p=6}}.</ref> sometimes called the '''golden field''',<ref>The name ''golden field'' was apparently introduced in 1988 by [[John Conway]] and [[Neil Sloane]] in the 1st edition of their book ''[[Sphere Packings, Lattices and Groups]]'' ([https://archive.org/details/spherepackingsla0000conw/page/207/mode/1up?q=%22golden+field%22 §{{nbsp}}8.2.1, {{pgs|207}}]). See {{harvnb|Conway|Sloane|1999}} for the 3rd edition. The name is relatively uncommon; most sources use symbolic names such as {{tmath|\Q(~\!\!\sqrt5~\!)}} or {{tmath|\Q(\varphi)}}.</ref> is a [[number]] system consisting of the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of all numbers {{tmath|a + b\sqrt5}}, where {{tmath|a}} and {{tmath|b}} are both [[rational numbers]] and {{tmath|\sqrt5}} is the [[square root of 5]], along with the basic [[Arithmetic#Operations|arithmetical operations]] (addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division). This arithmetic shares certain structural properties with the arithmetic of {{tmath|\Q}}, the [[field of rational numbers]], making {{Q(√5)}} also a type of [[field (mathematics)|field]]. More specifically, it is a [[real quadratic field]], the [[field extension|extension field]] of {{tmath|\Q}} generated by combining rational numbers and {{tmath|\sqrt5}} using arithmetical operations. The name comes from the [[golden ratio]] {{tmath|1= \varphi}}, a positive number satisfying the equation {{tmath|1=\textstyle \varphi^2 = \varphi + 1}}, which is the [[fundamental unit (number theory)|fundamental unit]] of {{Q(√5)}}.

Calculations in the golden field can be used to study the [[Fibonacci sequence|Fibonacci numbers]] and other topics related to the golden ratio, notably the [[geometry]] of the [[regular pentagon]] and higher-dimensional shapes with fivefold [[dihedral symmetry|symmetry]].

== Basic arithmetic ==

Elements of the golden field are those numbers which can be written in the form {{tmath|a + b\sqrt5}} where {{tmath|a}} and {{tmath|b}} are uniquely determined{{sfn|Lind|1968}} rational numbers, or in the form {{tmath|\bigl(a + b\sqrt5~\!\bigr)\big/ c}} where {{tmath|a}}, {{tmath|b}}, and {{tmath|c}} are integers, which can be uniquely [[Irreducible fraction|reduced to lowest terms]], and where {{tmath|1= \sqrt5 = 2.236\ldots}} is the [[square root of 5]].<ref name=A002163>{{harvnb|Sloane|at="Decimal expansion of square root of {{tmath|5}}", OEIS {{OEIS link | A002163}} }}.</ref> It is sometimes more convenient instead to use the form {{tmath|a + b\varphi}} where {{tmath|a}} and {{tmath|b}} are rational or the form {{tmath|(a + b\varphi)/c}} where {{tmath|a}}, {{tmath|b}}, and {{tmath|c}} are integers, and where <math>\varphi = \tfrac12\bigl(1 + \sqrt5~\!\bigr) = {}\!</math><math>1.618\ldots</math> is the [[golden ratio]].<ref name=A001622>{{harvnb|Sloane|at="Decimal expansion of golden ratio {{tmath|\varphi}} (or {{tmath|\tau}}) {{tmath|1= = (1 + \sqrt{5}~\!)/2}}", OEIS {{OEIS link | A001622}} }}.</ref>{{sfn|Dickson|1923|pp=129–130, 139}}

Converting between these alternative forms is straight-forward: {{tmath|1= a + b\sqrt5 = (a - b) + (2b)\varphi}} or, in the other direction, {{tmath|1= a + b\varphi = \bigl(a + \tfrac12 b\bigr) + \bigl(\tfrac12 b\bigr)\sqrt5}}.{{sfn|Dodd|1983|p=8}}

To [[addition|add]] or [[subtraction|subtract]] two numbers, simply add or subtract the components separately:{{sfn|Dimitrov|Cosklev|Bonevsky|1995}}
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\bigl(a_1 + b_1\sqrt5~\!\bigr) + \bigl(a_2 + b_2\sqrt5~\!\bigr) &= (a_1 + a_2) + (b_1 + b_2)\sqrt5, \\[3mu]
(a_1 + b_1\varphi) + (a_2 + b_2\varphi) &= (a_1 + a_2) + (b_1 + b_2)\varphi.
\end{align}</math>

To [[multiplication|multiply]] two numbers, [[FOIL method|distribute]]:{{sfn|Dimitrov|Cosklev|Bonevsky|1995}}
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\bigl(a_1 + b_1\sqrt5~\!\bigr) \bigl(a_2 + b_2\sqrt5~\!\bigr) &= (a_1a_2 + 5b_1b_2) + (a_1b_2 + b_1a_2)\sqrt5, \\[3mu]
(a_1 + b_1\varphi)(a_2 + b_2\varphi) &= (a_1a_2 + b_1b_2) + (a_1b_2 + b_1a_2 + b_1b_2)\varphi.
\end{align}</math>

To find the [[multiplicative inverse|reciprocal]] of a number <math>\alpha</math>, [[Rationalisation (mathematics)|rationalize]] the denominator: <math>1/\alpha = {}</math><math>\overline\alpha / \alpha \overline\alpha = {}</math>{{nobr|<math>\overline\alpha / \mathrm{N}(\alpha)</math>,}} where {{tmath|\overline\alpha}} is the algebraic conjugate and {{tmath|\mathrm N(\alpha)}} is the field norm, [[#Conjugation and norm|as defined below]].{{sfn|Dodd|1983|pp=9–10}} Explicitly:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\frac{1}{a + b\sqrt5} &= \frac{1}{a + b\sqrt5} \cdot \frac{a - b\sqrt5}{a - b\sqrt5} = \frac{a}{a^2 - 5b^2} - \frac{b}{a^2 - 5b^2}\sqrt5, \\[3mu]
\frac{1}{a + b\varphi} &= \frac{1}{a + b\varphi} \cdot \frac{a + b - b\varphi}{a + b - b\varphi} = \frac{a + b}{a^2 + ab - b^2 } - \frac{b}{a^2 + ab - b^2 }\varphi.
\end{align}</math>

To [[Division (mathematics)|divide]] two numbers, multiply the first by second's reciprocal:{{sfn|Dodd|1983|pp=9–10}}
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\frac{a_1 + b_1\sqrt5}{a_2 + b_2\sqrt5} &= \frac{a_1a_2 - 5b_1b_2}{a_2^2 - 5b_2^2} + \frac{-a_1b_2 + b_1a_2}{a_2^2 - 5b_2^2}\sqrt5, \\[6mu]
\frac{a_1 + b_1\varphi}{a_2 + b_2\varphi} &=  \frac{a_1a_2 + a_1b_2 - b_1b_2}{a_2^2 + a_2b_2 - b_2^2 } + \frac{-a_1b_2 + b_1a_2}{a_2^2 + a_2b_2 - b_2^2 }\varphi.
\end{align}</math>

[[Field (mathematics)#Definition|As in any field]], addition and multiplication of numbers in {{Q(√5)}} is [[associativity|associative]] and [[commutativity|commutative]]; {{tmath|0}} is the [[additive identity]] and {{tmath|1}} is the [[multiplicative identity]]; every number {{tmath|\alpha}} has an [[additive inverse]] {{tmath|-\alpha}} and a [[multiplicative inverse]] {{tmath|1/\alpha}}; and multiplication [[Distributivity|distributes]] over addition. Arithmetic between numbers in {{Q(√5)}} is consistent with their arithmetic as [[real number]]s; that is, {{Q(√5)}} is a [[subfield (mathematics)|subfield]] of {{tmath|\R}}.

== Conjugation and norm ==
The numbers {{tmath|\sqrt5}} and {{tmath|-\sqrt5}} each solve the equation {{tmath|1=\textstyle x^2 = 5}}. Each number {{tmath|1= \alpha = a + b\sqrt5}} in {{Q(√5)}} has an [[Conjugate element (field theory)|algebraic conjugate]] {{tmath|\overline\alpha}} found by swapping these two square roots of 5, i.e., by changing the sign of {{tmath|b}}. The conjugate of {{tmath|\varphi}} is <math>\overline\varphi = \tfrac12\bigl(1 - \sqrt5~\!\bigr) = {}</math><math>\textstyle -\varphi^{-1} = {}</math>{{nobr|<math>1 - \varphi</math>}}. A rational number is its own conjugate, {{tmath|1= a = \overline a}}. In general, the conjugate is:{{sfn|Dodd|1983|pp=8–9}}
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\overline{a + b\sqrt5} &= a - b\sqrt5, \\[3mu]
\overline{a + b\varphi} &= a + b\overline\varphi = (a + b) - b\varphi.
\end{align}</math>
Conjugation in {{Q(√5)}} is an [[Involution (mathematics)|involution]], {{tmath|1= \overline{(\overline\alpha)} = \alpha }}, and it preserves the structure of arithmetic: {{tmath|1= \overline{\alpha_1 + \alpha_2} = \overline\alpha_1 +\overline\alpha_2 }}; {{tmath|1= \overline{\alpha_1\alpha_2} = \overline\alpha_1 \overline\alpha_2 }}; and {{tmath|1= \overline{\alpha_1 /\alpha_2} = \overline\alpha_1 /\, \overline\alpha_2 }}.{{sfn|Dodd|1983|p=9}} Conjugation is the only [[ring homomorphism]] (function preserving the structure of addition and multiplication) from {{Q(√5)}} to itself, other than the [[identity function]].<ref>This is true for conjugation in quadratic fields in general. See {{harvnb|Trifković|2013|p=62}}.</ref>

The [[field trace]] is the sum of a number and its conjugates (so-called because multiplication by an element in the field can be seen as a kind of linear transformation, the [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]] of [[#Matrix representation|whose matrix]] is the field trace).{{sfn|Rotman|2017}} The trace of {{tmath|\alpha}} in {{Q(√5)}} is {{tmath|1= \mathrm{tr}(\alpha) = \alpha + \overline\alpha}}:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\mathrm{tr}\bigl(a + b\sqrt5~\!\bigr) &= \bigl(a + b\sqrt5~\!\bigr) + \bigl(a - b\sqrt5~\!\bigr) = 2a, \\[3mu]
\mathrm{tr}(a + b\varphi) &= (a + b\varphi) + (a + b - b\varphi) = 2a + b.
\end{align}</math>
This is always an (ordinary) rational number.{{sfn|Dodd|1983|p=9}}

The [[field norm]] is a measure of a number's magnitude, the product of the number and its conjugates.{{sfn|Appleby|Bengtsson|Grassl|Harrison|2022}} The norm of {{tmath|\alpha}} in {{Q(√5)}} is {{tmath|1= \mathrm{N}(\alpha) = \alpha\overline\alpha}}:{{sfn|Dodd|1983|p=9}}
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\mathrm{N}\bigl(a + b\sqrt5~\!\bigr) &= a^2 - 5b^2, \\[3mu]
\mathrm{N}(a + b\varphi) &= a^2 + ab - b^2.
\end{align}</math>
This is also always a rational number.{{sfn|Dodd|1983|p=9}}

The norm preserves the structure of multiplication, as expected for a concept of magnitude. The norm of a product is the product of norms, {{tmath|1= \operatorname{N}(\alpha_1 \alpha_2) = \mathrm{N}(\alpha_1)~\!\mathrm{N}(\alpha_2)\!}}; and the norm of a quotient is the quotient of the norms, {{tmath|1= \mathrm{N}(\alpha_1/\alpha_2) = \mathrm{N}(\alpha_1)\big/~\!\mathrm{N}(\alpha_2)}}. A number and its conjugate have the same norm, {{tmath|1= \mathrm{N}(\alpha) = \mathrm{N}(\overline\alpha)}}.{{sfn|Dodd|1983|p=9}}

A number {{tmath|\alpha}} in {{Q(√5)}} and its conjugate {{tmath|\overline\alpha}} are the solutions of the [[quadratic equation]]{{sfn|Dodd|1983|p=9}}
<math display=block>
(x - \alpha)(x - \overline\alpha)
= x^2 - \mathrm{tr}(\alpha)x + \mathrm{N}(\alpha) = 0.
</math>

In [[Galois theory]], the golden field can be considered more abstractly as the set of all numbers {{tmath|a + bu}}, where {{tmath|a}} and {{tmath|b}} are both rational, and all that is known of {{tmath|u}} is that it satisfies the equation {{tmath|1=\textstyle u^2 = 5}}. There are two ways to embed this set in the real numbers: by mapping {{tmath|u}} to the positive square root {{tmath|\sqrt5}} or alternatively by mapping {{tmath|u}} to the negative square root {{tmath|-\sqrt5}}. Conjugation exchanges these two embeddings. The [[Galois group]] of the golden field is thus the [[group (mathematics)|group]] with two elements, namely the identity and an element which is its own inverse.{{sfn|Appleby|Bengtsson|Grassl|Harrison|2022}}

== Golden integers ==
[[File:Golden integer lattice.png |thumb |upright=1.5 |One convenient way to plot {{math|'''Z'''[''φ'']}} is as a [[Lattice (group)|lattice]] in the [[real coordinate plane]]. The so-called ''canonical embedding'' represents the number {{math|''α''}} by the point with coordinates {{math|1={{pars|''α'', ''{{overline|α}}''|110%}}}}. Numbers with the same norm lie on [[hyperbola]]s (orange and green lines).]]
[[File:Golden integer lattice, logarithmic embedding.png |thumb |upright=1.25 |right |The ''logarithmic embedding'' into the plane represents the (non-zero) number {{math|''α''}} by the point with coordinates {{math|1={{pars|{{hairsp}}log{{thinsp}}{{abs|''α''}}, log{{thinsp}}{{abs|''{{overline|α}}''}}|110%}}}} – See [[Log–log plot]]. Multiplication in the golden field corresponds to [[vector addition]] in the embedding. Numbers whose norm has the same absolute value lie on diagonal lines.]]
The [[ring of integers]] of the golden field, {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}}, sometimes called the '''golden integers''',<ref>For instance by {{harvnb|Rokhsar|Mermin|Wright|1987}}; {{harvnb|Lehrer|Taylor|2009|p=253}}.</ref> is the set of all [[algebraic integer]]s in the field, meaning those elements whose [[Minimal polynomial (field theory)|minimal polynomial]] over {{tmath|\Q}} has integer coefficients. These are the set of numbers in {{Q(√5)}} whose norm and trace are integers. The numbers {{tmath|1}} and {{tmath|\varphi}} form an [[integral basis]] for the ring, meaning every number in the ring can be written in the form <math>a + b\varphi</math> where <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are [[integer|ordinary integers]].{{sfnm|1a1=Hirzebruch|1y=1976 |2a1=Sporn|2y=2021}} Alternately, elements of {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}} can be written in the form {{tmath|\tfrac12a + \tfrac12b\sqrt5}}, where {{tmath|a}} and {{tmath|b}} have the same [[Parity (mathematics)|parity]].{{sfn|Dodd|1983|p=11}} Like any ring, {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}} is closed under addition and multiplication. {{Q(√5)}} is the smallest field containing {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}}, its [[field of fractions]].

=== Norms ===

The set of all norms of golden integers includes every number <math>\textstyle a^2 + ab - b^2 ={}\! </math><math>\mathrm{N}(a + b\varphi)</math> for ordinary integers {{tmath|a}} and {{tmath|b}}.{{sfn|Dodd|1983|pp=28–29}} These are precisely the ordinary integers whose ordinary prime factors which are congruent to {{tmath|\pm 2}} [[Modular arithmetic|modulo]] {{tmath|5}} occur with even exponents (see {{slink||Primes and prime factorization}} below).{{sfn|Dodd|1983|pp=26–28}} The first several non-negative integer norms are:<ref>{{harvnb|Sloane|at="Positive numbers of the form {{tmath|\textstyle x^2 + xy - y^2}}", OEIS {{OEIS link | A031363}} }}.</ref>
: {{tmath|0}}, {{tmath|1}}, {{tmath|4}}, {{tmath|5}}, {{tmath|9}}, {{tmath|11}}, {{tmath|16}}, {{tmath|19}}, {{tmath|20}}, {{tmath|25}}, {{tmath|29}},{{nobr| .{{hairsp}}.{{hairsp}}.{{thinsp}}.}}

The golden integer {{tmath|1= 0 = 0 + 0\varphi}} is called ''zero'', and is the only element of {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}} with norm {{tmath|0}}.{{sfn|Dodd|1983|p=3}}

=== Divisibility ===

If {{tmath|\alpha}} and {{tmath|\beta}} are golden integers and there is some golden integer {{tmath|\gamma}} such that {{tmath|1= \alpha\gamma = \beta}}, we say that {{tmath|\alpha}} [[divisor|''divides'']] {{tmath|\beta}}, denoted {{tmath|\alpha \mid \beta}}. In many respects, [[Divisibility (ring theory)|divisibility]] works similarly as among the ordinary integers, but with some important differences, as will be described in the following subsections.

Because, like the integers, {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}} is an [[integral domain]], the product of two non-zero elements is always non-zero. Thus {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}} has no [[nontrivial zero divisor]]s, and {{tmath|1= \alpha\beta = 0}} implies that either {{tmath|1= \alpha = 0}} or {{tmath|1= \beta = 0}}.

=== Units ===
A ''[[unit (ring theory)|unit]]'' is an algebraic integer which divides {{tmath|1}}, i.e. whose multiplicative inverse is also an algebraic integer, which happens when its norm is {{tmath|\pm 1}}. Among the ordinary integers, the units are the pair of numbers {{tmath|\pm1}}, but among the golden integers there are infinitely many units: all numbers of the form {{tmath|a + b\varphi}} whose integer coefficients {{tmath|a}} and {{tmath|b}} solve the [[Diophantine equation]] {{tmath|1=\textstyle a^2 + ab - b^2 = \pm1}}. If a unit is instead written in the form {{tmath|\tfrac12a + \tfrac12b\sqrt5}}, its coefficients solve a related Diophantine equation, the [[generalized Pell's equation]] {{tmath|1=\textstyle  a^2 -5b^2 = \pm4}}. The [[Fundamental unit (number theory)|fundamental unit]] – the smallest unit greater than {{tmath|1}} – is the [[golden ratio]] {{tmath|1=\varphi = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\sqrt5}} and the other units consist of its positive and negative powers, {{tmath|\pm\varphi^n}}, for any integer {{tmath|n}}.{{sfn|Lind|1968}} Some [[Golden ratio#Golden ratio conjugate and powers|powers of {{tmath|\varphi}}]] are:

In general {{tmath|1=\textstyle \varphi^{n} = F_{n-1} + F_n\varphi }}, where {{tmath|F_n}} is the {{tmath|n}}th [[#Fibonacci numbers|Fibonacci number]].<ref>{{harvnb|Wasteels|1902}}; {{harvnb|Dodd|1983|p=22}}; {{harvnb|Dimitrov|Cosklev|Bonevsky|1995}}.</ref> The units form the [[group (mathematics)|group]] {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]^\times\!}} under multiplication, which can be decomposed as the [[Direct product of groups|direct product]] of a [[cyclic group]] of order 2 generated by {{tmath|-1}} and an infinite cyclic group generated by {{tmath|\varphi}}.

=== Associates ===

Two golden integers {{tmath|\alpha_1}} and {{tmath|\alpha_2}} are ''[[associated element|associates]]'' if each divides the other, {{tmath|\alpha_1 \mid \alpha_2}} and {{tmath|\alpha_2 \mid \alpha_1}}. Equivalently, their quotient in {{tmath|\Q(\varphi)}} is a unit, {{tmath|1= \alpha_2 = \pm\varphi^n\alpha_1 }} for some integer {{tmath |n}}. Associateness is an [[equivalence relation]]. If {{tmath|\alpha_1}} divides some golden integer {{tmath|\beta}}, then so does its associate {{tmath|\alpha_2}}: if {{tmath|\alpha_1 \mid \beta}} then {{tmath|\alpha_2 \mid \beta}}.

Associates have the same norm, up to sign: {{nobr|<math>|\mathrm{N}(\alpha_1)| = |\mathrm{N}(\alpha_2)|</math>.}} However, not all elements whose norm has the same absolute value are associates; in particular, any golden-integer prime and its conjugate have the same norm, but are associates if and only if they are associated either with {{tmath|\sqrt 5}} or with an ordinary prime.{{sfn|Dodd|1983|pp=26–28}} 

More generally, two numbers in {{Q(√5)}} are associates if their quotient is a unit. The set of associates of any number in {{Q(√5)}} is the [[orbit (group theory)|orbit]] of any of them under the multiplicative [[group action|action]] of the group of units.

=== Primes and prime factorization ===
[[File:Golden integer primes.png |thumb |upright=1.25 |Golden integer units (hollow circles) and primes (filled circles), along with zero (+) and composite numbers (×)<ref name=doddprimes>A list of primes can be found in {{harvnb|Dodd|1983|at=Appendix B, "A List of Primes", {{pgs|128–150}} }}.</ref>]]
A [[prime element]] of a ring, analogous to a [[prime number]] among the integers, is an element {{tmath|\gamma}} such that whenever {{tmath|\gamma \mid \alpha\beta}}, then either {{tmath|\gamma \mid \alpha}} or {{tmath|\gamma \mid \beta}}. In {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}} the primes are of three types: {{tmath|1= \sqrt5 = -1 + 2\varphi}}, integer primes of the form {{tmath|1= p = 5n \pm 2}}<ref>{{harvnb|Sloane|at="Primes congruent to {{tmath|2}} or {{tmath|3}} modulo {{tmath|5}}", OEIS {{OEIS link|A003631}} }}.</ref> where {{tmath|n}} is an integer, and the factors of integer primes of the form {{tmath|1= p = 5n \pm 1}}<ref>{{harvnb|Sloane|at="Primes congruent to {{tmath| \{1,\,4\} }} mod {{tmath|5}}", OEIS {{OEIS link| A045468}} }}.</ref> (a pair of conjugates).{{sfn|Hardy|Wright|1954|pp=221–222}} For example, {{tmath|2}}, {{tmath|3}}, and {{tmath|7}} are primes, but {{tmath|1= 11 = (3 + \varphi)(4 - \varphi)}} is composite. Any of these is an associate of additional primes; for example {{tmath|2\varphi}} is also prime, an associate of {{tmath|2}}.{{r|doddprimes}}

The ring {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}} is a [[Euclidean domain]] with the absolute value of the norm as its Euclidean function, meaning a version of the [[Euclidean algorithm]] can be used to find the [[greatest common divisor]] of two numbers.{{sfn|Dodd|1983|at=Ch. 2, [https://archive.org/details/numbertheoryinqu0000dodd/page/7 "Elementary Divisibility Properties of {{math|Z(ω)}}"], {{pgs|7–19}}}} This makes {{Q(√5)}} one of the 21 [[quadratic field]]s that are [[norm-Euclidean field|norm-Euclidean]].<ref>{{harvnb|LeVeque |1956 |at=[https://archive.org/details/topicsinnumberth02leve/page/56/mode/2up {{pgs|56–57}}]}}; {{harvnb|Sloane|at="Squarefree values of {{tmath|n}} for which the quadratic field {{tmath|\mathbf{Q}[\sqrt{n}~\!]}} is norm-Euclidean", OEIS {{OEIS link |A048981}} }}.</ref> A form of the [[fundamental theorem of arithmetic]] applies in {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}}: every golden integer can be written as a product of prime elements multiplied by a unit, and this factorization is unique [[up to]] the order of the factors and the replacement of any prime factor by one of its associates (which changes the unit factor accordingly).

=== Ideals ===

An [[ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] of {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}} is any subset which "absorbs multiplication", containing every golden-integer multiple of each of its elements. If {{tmath|\alpha}} is any golden integer, the set of all golden-integer multiples of {{tmath|\alpha}}, denoted {{tmath|\alpha\Z[\varphi]}} or {{tmath|(\alpha)}}, is the ideal [[generating set of an ideal|generated by]] {{tmath|\alpha}}. Every associated element generates the same ideal, but a non-associated element generates a different ideal: that is, {{tmath|1= (\alpha) = (\beta)}} [[If and only if|precisely when]] {{tmath|1=\textstyle \alpha = \pm\beta\varphi^n}}. Because {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}} is a [[principal ideal domain]], each ideal of {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}} can be generated by a single element. The zero ideal {{tmath|(0)}} is the single-element set {{tmath| \{ 0\} }}. The ideal {{tmath|(1)}} is all of {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}}.

[[Ideal (ring theory)#Ideal operations|Various operations]] can be defined among ideals. If {{tmath|\mathfrak a}} and {{tmath|\mathfrak b}} are ideals of {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}}, then {{tmath|\mathfrak{a} + \mathfrak{b} }} is the set of all sums of one element in {{tmath|\mathfrak a}} plus one element in {{tmath|\mathfrak b}}, and {{tmath|\mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b} }} is the set of all sums of any number of terms, each of which is the product of one element in {{tmath|\mathfrak a}} times one element in {{tmath|\mathfrak b}}.
<math display=block>\begin{align}
 \! \mathfrak{a} + \mathfrak{b} &= \{\,\alpha + \beta \mid \alpha \in \mathfrak{a},\, \beta \in \mathfrak{b} \,\}, \\[3mu]
 \! \mathfrak{a} \mathfrak{b} &= \bigl\{\, {\textstyle \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i\beta_i} \mathrel{\big|} n \in \N,\, a_i \in \mathfrak{a},\, b_i \in \mathfrak{b} \,\bigr\}.
\end{align}</math>
The sum or product of two ideals is itself an ideal. Multiplication of ideals is distributive over addition.

More generally, a [[fractional ideal]] of {{Q(√5)}} is a subset of {{Q(√5)}} with the property that multiplication of each element by some golden integer, the "denominator", results in an ideal of {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}}. If {{tmath|\alpha}} is any number in {{Q(√5)}}, the set of golden-integer multiples of {{tmath|\alpha}}, also denoted {{tmath|\alpha\Z[\varphi]}} or {{tmath|(\alpha)}}, is the fractional ideal generated by {{tmath|\alpha}}. As with integral ideals of {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}}, numbers in {{Q(√5)}} generate the same fractional ideal if and only if they are associated, and every fractional ideal can be generated by a single element. Multiplication of fractional ideals is consistent with multiplication of their generators. Let {{tmath|\textstyle \Q\bigl(\sqrt5~\!\bigr)\vphantom)^{~\!\!\times} }} be the multiplicative group of the nonzero elements of {{Q(√5)}}, and {{tmath|U}} be the group of the units. The function that maps each element of {{tmath|\Q\bigl(\sqrt5~\!\bigr)\vphantom)^{~\!\!\times} }} to the generated fractional ideal, {{tmath| \alpha \mapsto (\alpha)}}, induces a [[group isomorphism]] between {{tmath|\Q\bigl(\sqrt5~\!\bigr)\vphantom)^{~\!\!\times}\! \big/ U}} and the group of fractional ideals.

=== Table of integers ===

In the table below, positive golden integers have been arranged into rows, with one representative chosen for each class of associates (here the representative is the positive element {{tmath|\alpha}} in the class for which <math>\alpha + | \overline\alpha | </math> is a minimum).{{r|doddprimes}} The units {{tmath|\pm\varphi^n}} (associates of {{tmath|1}}) and the number {{tmath|1= \sqrt5 = -1 + 2\varphi}} and its associates {{tmath|\pm\sqrt5\,\varphi^n}} appear often in applications.

== Matrix representation ==

{{Q(√5)}} is a two-dimensional [[vector space]] over {{tmath|\Q}}, and multiplication by any element of {{Q(√5)}} is a [[linear transformation]] of that vector space. Given an ordered [[Basis (linear algebra)|basis]] of {{Q(√5)}}, each number in {{Q(√5)}} can be associated to the corresponding [[transformation matrix]] in that basis. This defines a field [[isomorphism]] (a structure-preserving [[bijective map]]) from {{Q(√5)}} to the space of {{tmath|2 \times 2}} square [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] with rational entries [[Linear span|spanned]] by the [[identity matrix]] {{tmath|\mathbf I}}, the image of the number {{tmath|1}}, and a matrix {{tmath|\mathbf\Phi}}, the image of {{tmath|\varphi}}.{{r|matrices}} Thus arithmetic of numbers in {{Q(√5)}} can be alternately represented by [[Matrix arithmetic|the arithmetic]] of such matrices.<ref name=rotman>{{harvnb|Rotman|2017|p=456 ff.}} describes this for finite-dimensional field extensions in general.</ref> In this context, the number {{tmath|1= \alpha = a + b\varphi}} is represented by the matrix {{tmath|1= \mathbf A = a\mathbf I + b \mathbf \Phi}}.{{sfn|Boukas|Feinsilver|Fellouris|2016}} A convenient choice of basis for {{Q(√5)}} is {{tmath|( 1, \varphi) }}, in terms of which {{tmath|\mathbf\Phi}} is a [[symmetric matrix]]:<ref>Our matrix {{tmath|\mathbf\Phi}}, or the mirrored variant {{tmath| \bigl[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix} \bigr]}}, is commonly denoted {{tmath|\mathbf Q}} or {{tmath|\mathcal Q}} in work about the Fibonacci numbers. See {{harvnb|Gould|1981}} for a survey in that context. Here we use the symbol {{tmath|\mathbf \Phi}} for consistency with the symbol {{tmath|\varphi}} and to avoid confusion with the rational numbers {{tmath|\Q}}, which are also often denoted {{tmath|\mathbf Q}}. {{harvnb|Liba|Ilany|2023|p=15}} also use the symbol {{tmath|\mathbf\Phi}}, and call this the "golden matrix".</ref>
<math display=block>\begin{align}
& \mathbf I = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf\Phi = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf A = a\mathbf I + b\mathbf\Phi = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ b & a + b \end{bmatrix}. \quad
\end{align}</math>

The [[adjugate matrix]] {{tmath|1= \overline{\mathbf\Phi} = \mathbf I - \mathbf\Phi }} represents the algebraic conjugate {{tmath|1= \overline\varphi = 1 - \varphi}}, the matrix {{tmath|1=\mathbf R = -\mathbf I + 2\mathbf\Phi}} (satisfying {{tmath|1=\textstyle \mathbf R^2 = 5 \mathbf I}}) represents {{tmath|\sqrt5}},<ref>{{harvnb|Hoggatt|Ruggles|1963}}; {{harvnb|Liba|Ilany|2023|p=16}}</ref> and the adjugate of an arbitrary element {{tmath|\mathbf A}}, which we will denote {{tmath|1= \overline{\mathbf A} = a\mathbf I + b \overline{\mathbf\Phi} }}, represents the number {{tmath|1= \overline\alpha = a + b\overline\varphi}}:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
& \mathbf R = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\overline{\mathbf\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} ~1 & -1 \\ -1 & \,0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
\overline{\mathbf A} = a\mathbf I + b\overline{\mathbf\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} a+b & -b~ \\ -b & ~a \end{bmatrix}.
\end{align}</math>

Every matrix {{tmath|1= \mathbf A = a\mathbf I + b \mathbf \Phi}}, except for the [[zero matrix]], is [[invertible matrix|invertible]], and its inverse {{tmath|1=\textstyle \mathbf A^{-1} = \bigl(1/\mathrm{det}(\mathbf A)\bigr) \overline{\mathbf A} }} represents the multiplicative inverse {{tmath|1= \textstyle \alpha^{-1} = \overline\alpha / \mathrm{N}(\alpha) }} in {{Q(√5)}}.{{sfn|Liba|Ilany|2023|p=14}}

If {{tmath|1= \alpha = a + b\varphi}} is an element of {{Q(√5)}}, with conjugate {{tmath|1= \overline\alpha = a + b\overline\varphi }}, then the matrix {{tmath|1= \mathbf A = a\mathbf I + b\mathbf \Phi}} has the numbers {{tmath|\alpha}}  and {{tmath|\overline\alpha}} as its [[eigenvalue]]s. Its [[trace (linear algebra)|trace]] is <math> \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf A) = {}\!</math><math>2a + b = {}\!</math>{{nobr|<math>\mathrm{tr}(\alpha)</math>.<ref>Here {{tmath|\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf A)}} means the [[matrix trace]] of {{tmath|\mathbf A}} and {{tmath|\mathrm{tr}(\alpha)}} means the [[field trace]] of {{tmath|\alpha}} in {{tmath|\Q(\sqrt5~\!)}}.</ref>}} Its [[determinant]] is <math>\mathrm{det}(\mathbf A) = {}\!</math><math>\textstyle a^2 + ab - b^2 = {}\!</math>{{nobr|<math>\mathrm{N}(\alpha)</math>.}} The [[characteristic polynomial]] of {{tmath|\mathbf A}} is {{tmath|(x - \alpha)(x - \overline\alpha)}}, which is the minimal polynomial of {{tmath|\alpha}} and {{tmath|\overline\alpha}} whenever {{tmath|b}} is not zero. These properties are shared by the adjugate matrix {{tmath|\overline{\mathbf A} }}. Their product is {{tmath|1= \mathbf A \overline{\mathbf A} = \mathrm{det}(\mathbf A)\mathbf I }}.{{r|rotman}}<ref name=matrices>{{harvnb|Liba|Ilany|2023|p=15}}; {{harvnb|Yang|1997}}; {{harvnb|Fontaine|Hurley|2011}} also mention the isomorphism between the real subfield of the cyclotomic field {{tmath|\Q(\zeta)}} and the arithmetic of matrices spanned by {{tmath|\mathbf I}} and {{tmath|\mathbf\Phi}}, which they call the ''silver matrices'' {{tmath|S[5,1]}} and {{tmath|S[5,2]}}. {{pb}} {{harvnb|Méndez-Delgadillo|Lam-Estrada|Maldonado-Ramírez|2015}} work with the basis {{tmath|(~\!\!\sqrt5, 1) }}, relative to which the matrix {{tmath|\mathbf R'}} represents {{tmath|\sqrt5}}: {{pb}} <math>\begin{align}
\quad & \mathbf R' = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 5 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \ \ 
a\mathbf I + b \mathbf R' = \begin{bmatrix} a & 5b \\ b & a \end{bmatrix}.
\end{align}</math> {{pb}}
In this basis, the golden ratio {{tmath|\varphi}} is represented by a matrix {{tmath|1= \mathbf\Phi'\!\!~ = \tfrac12\mathbf I + \tfrac12\mathbf R'}}: {{pb}} <math>\begin{align}
\quad& \mathbf\Phi'\!\!~ = \begin{bmatrix} \tfrac12 & \!\!\tfrac52 \\ \tfrac12 & \!\!\tfrac12 \end{bmatrix}, \ \ 
a\mathbf I + b \mathbf \Phi'\!\!~ = \begin{bmatrix} a ~\!{+}~\! \tfrac12b & \tfrac52b \,\, \\ \,\tfrac12b & \!\! a ~\!{+}~\! \tfrac12b \end{bmatrix}.
\end{align}</math> {{pb}} This is the same idea as using the matrices {{tmath|\mathbf R}} and {{tmath|\mathbf\Phi}}: arithmetic of these matrices is likewise isomorphic to arithmetic in {{tmath|\Q(\sqrt5~\!)}}, and the eigenvalues, characteristic polynomial, trace, and determinant are the same in any basis. However, the [[eigenvector]]s are {{tmath|1=\textstyle \begin{bmatrix} ~\!\!\sqrt5 & \!1 \end{bmatrix}{}^\mathsf{T} }} and {{tmath|1=\textstyle \begin{bmatrix} -\sqrt5 & \!1 \end{bmatrix}{}^\mathsf{T} }} rather than {{tmath|1=\textstyle \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \!\varphi \end{bmatrix}{}^\mathsf{T} }} and {{tmath|1=\textstyle \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \!\overline\varphi \end{bmatrix}{}^\mathsf{T} \!}}.</ref>

These matrices have especially been studied in the context of the [[#Fibonacci numbers|Fibonacci numbers]] {{tmath|F_n}} and [[#Fibonacci numbers|Lucas numbers]] {{tmath|L_n}}, which appear as the entries of {{tmath|\textstyle \mathbf\Phi^n}} and {{tmath|\textstyle \mathbf\Phi^n \mathbf R}}, respectively:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\mathbf\Phi^n &= F_{n-1}\mathbf I + F_n\mathbf\Phi = \begin{bmatrix} F_{n-1} & F_n~ \\ F_n~ & F_{n+1} \end{bmatrix}, & \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf\Phi^n) &= L_n, \\[8mu]
\mathbf\Phi^n\mathbf R &= L_{n-1}\mathbf I + L_n\mathbf\Phi = \begin{bmatrix} L_{n-1} & L_n~ \\ L_n~ & L_{n+1} \end{bmatrix}, & \mathrm{tr}(\mathbf\Phi^n\mathbf R) &= 5F_n.
\end{align}</math>
Powers of {{tmath|\mathbf\Phi}} are sometimes called ''Fibonacci matrices''.<ref>{{harvnb|Bicknell|Hoggatt|1973|pp=18–26}}; {{harvnb|Gould|1981}}.</ref>

Every matrix of the form {{tmath|1= a\mathbf I + b\mathbf \Phi}} has [[eigenvectors]] which point along the directions {{tmath|1=\textstyle \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \!\varphi \end{bmatrix}{}^\mathsf{T} }} and {{tmath|1=\textstyle \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \!\overline\varphi \end{bmatrix}{}^\mathsf{T} \!}}.<ref>Here the symbol {{tmath|\mathsf{T} }} indicates the [[transpose]] of a matrix, so {{tmath|1=\textstyle \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \!\varphi \end{bmatrix}{}^\mathsf{T} }} is a [[column vector]].</ref> When numbers in {{Q(√5)}} are plotted, [[#Golden integers|as above]], in a coordinate system where their values as real numbers are the horizontal axis and the values of their conjugates are the vertical axis, the eigenvectors point along those two axes. (Zero is the only number {{Q(√5)}} directly ''on'' either axis.) The matrices {{tmath|\mathbf \Phi^{2n} }} for integer {{tmath|n}}, representing units, and more generally any matrices with {{tmath|a + b\varphi > 0}} and determinant {{tmath|1}}, are [[squeeze mapping]]s, which stretch the plane along one axis and squish it along the other, fixing hyperbolas of constant norm. The matrices {{tmath|\mathbf \Phi^{2n + 1} }} and more generally matrices with {{tmath|a + b\varphi > 0}} and determinant {{tmath|-1}}, are the composition of a squeeze mapping and a vertical [[Reflection (mathematics)|reflection]]. The negative identity matrix {{tmath|- \mathbf I}} is a [[point reflection]] across the origin. In general any other matrix {{tmath|1= a\mathbf I + b\mathbf \Phi}} can be decomposed as the product of a squeeze mapping, possibly a reflection, and a uniform scaling by the square root of the absolute value of its determinant.

== Other properties ==
The golden field is the real quadratic field with the smallest [[Discriminant of an algebraic number field|discriminant]], {{tmath|1= \Delta_{\Q\left(~\!\!\sqrt5\right)} = 5}}.{{sfn|Dembélé|2005}} It has [[Class number (number theory)|class number]] 1, which means that the ring of its algebraic integers is a [[principal ideal domain]] and a [[unique factorization domain]].<ref>{{harvnb|Sloane|at="{{tmath|\mathbf{Q}(\sqrt{n})}} is a unique factorization domain", OEIS {{OEIS link |A003172}} }}</ref>

Any positive element of the golden field can be written as a generalized type of [[continued fraction]], in which the partial quotients are sums of non-negative powers of <math>\varphi</math>.{{sfn|Bernat|2006}}

== Fibonacci numbers ==
[[File:Fibonacci and Lucas numbers as powers of the golden ratio.png |upright=1.25 |thumb |The Lucas and Fibonacci numbers are components of {{math|''φ''<sup>''n''</sup>}} when written in terms of {{math|{{sfrac|1|2}}}} and {{math|{{sfrac|1|2}}√5}}.<ref>{{harvnb|Vajda|1989|p=31}} plots these points and hyperbolas rotated and scaled so that {{tmath|\tfrac12}} and {{tmath|\tfrac12\sqrt5}} coordinates make a square grid aligned with the page.</ref>]]

{{Q(√5)}} is a natural choice of number system for studying the [[Fibonacci sequence|Fibonacci numbers]] {{tmath|F_n}} and the [[Lucas number]]s {{tmath|L_n}}. These number sequences are usually defined by [[recurrence relation]]s similar to the one satisfied by the powers of {{tmath|\varphi}} and {{tmath|\overline\varphi}}:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
F_0 &= 0,& F_1 &= 1,& F_{n+1} &= F_n + F_{n-1}, \\[3mu]
L_0 &= 2,& L_1 &= 1,& L_{n+1} &= L_n + L_{n-1}, \\[3mu]
\varphi^0 &= 1,
  & \varphi^1 &= \varphi,
  & \varphi^{n+1} &= \varphi^{n} + \varphi^{n-1}, \\[3mu]
\overline\varphi^0 &= 1,
  & \overline\varphi^1 &= \overline\varphi,
  & \overline\varphi^{n+1} &= \overline\varphi^{n} + \overline\varphi^{n-1}.
\end{align}</math>

The sequences {{tmath|F_n}} and {{tmath|L_n}} respectively begin:<ref>{{harvnb|Sloane|at="Fibonacci numbers", OEIS {{OEIS link |A000045}} }}; {{harvnb|Sloane|at="Lucas numbers beginning at {{tmath|2}}", OEIS {{OEIS link |A000032}} }}.</ref>

|}

Both sequences can be consistently extended to negative integer indices by following the same recurrence in the negative direction. They satisfy the identities<ref>{{harvnb|Vajda|1989|p=10}}; {{harvnb|Sloane|at="[...] Fibonacci numbers extended to negative indices", OEIS {{OEIS link | A039834}} }}.</ref>
<math display=block>\begin{align}
F_{-n} &= (-1)^{n+1} F_n, \\
L_{-n} &= (-1)^{n} L_n.
\end{align}</math>

The Fibonacci and Lucas numbers can alternately be expressed as the components {{tmath|b}} and {{tmath|a}} when a power of the golden ratio or its conjugate is written in the form {{tmath|\tfrac12a + \tfrac12b\sqrt5}}:<ref>{{harvnb|Lind|1968}}; {{harvnb|Vajda|1989|p=52}}</ref>
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\varphi^n &= \tfrac12L_n + \tfrac12F_n\sqrt5, \\[3mu]
\overline\varphi^n &= \tfrac12L_n - \tfrac12F_n\sqrt5.
\end{align}</math>

[[File:Fibonacci numbers in the golden integer lattice.png |thumb |upright=1.25 |Binet's formula for Fibonacci numbers plotted in the lattice of golden integers]]

The expression of the Fibonacci numbers in terms of {{tmath|\varphi}} is called [[Binet's formula]]:<ref>{{harvnb|Dodd|1983|p=5}}. {{pb}} The formula was developed by [[Abraham de Moivre]] (1718) and then independently by [[Jacques Philippe Marie Binet]] (1843) and [[Gabriel Lamé]] (1844); see {{harvnb|Vajda|1989|p=52}}.</ref>

<math display=block>\begin{align}
F_n &= \frac{\varphi^n - \overline\varphi^n}{\varphi - \overline\varphi}
     = \frac{\varphi^n - \overline\varphi^n }{\sqrt5 }
     = \frac{ \mathrm{tr}\bigl(\varphi^n\sqrt5~\!\bigr)}{5}, \\[5mu]
L_n &= \frac{\varphi^n + \overline\varphi^n}{\varphi + \overline\varphi}
     = \varphi^n + \overline\varphi^n
     = \mathrm{tr}{\left(\varphi^n\right)}.
\end{align}</math>

The powers of {{tmath|\varphi}} or {{tmath|\overline\varphi}}, when written in the form {{tmath|a + b\varphi}}, can be expressed in terms of just Fibonacci numbers,{{sfn|Dodd|1983|p=22}}
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\varphi^n &= F_{n-1} + F_n\varphi, \\[3mu]
\overline\varphi^n &= F_{n-1} + F_n\overline\varphi = F_{n+1} - F_n\varphi.
\end{align}</math>
Powers of {{tmath|\varphi}} or {{tmath|\overline\varphi}} times {{tmath|\sqrt5}} can be expressed in terms of just Lucas numbers,
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\varphi^n\sqrt5 &= L_{n-1} + L_n\varphi, \\[3mu]
\overline\varphi^n\sqrt5 &= - L_{n-1} - L_n\overline\varphi = -L_{n+1} + L_n\varphi.
\end{align}</math>
Statements about golden integers can be recast as statements about the Fibonacci or Lucas numbers; for example, that every power of {{tmath|\varphi}} is a unit of {{tmath|\Z[\varphi]}}, {{tmath|1=\textstyle \mathrm{N}(\varphi^n) = {\mathrm{N}(\varphi)}^n = {(-1)}^n}}, when expanded, becomes [[Cassini's identity]], and likewise {{tmath|1=\textstyle \mathrm{N}(\varphi^n\sqrt5) = {\mathrm{N}(\varphi)}^n\mathrm{N}\bigl(\sqrt5\bigr) = {(-1)}^n5}} becomes the analogous identity about Lucas numbers,
<math display=block>\begin{align}
(F_{n-1} + F_n\varphi)(F_{n+1} - F_n\varphi) &= F_{n-1}F_{n+1} - F_n^2 = (-1)^n, \\[3mu]
(L_{n-1} + L_n\varphi)(-L_{n+1} + L_n\varphi) &= L_n^2 - L_{n-1}L_{n+1} = (-1)^n5.
\end{align}</math>

The numbers {{tmath|\textstyle \varphi^n}} and {{tmath|\textstyle \overline\varphi^n}} are the roots of the quadratic polynomial {{tmath|1=\textstyle x^2 - L_nx + (-1)^n }}. This is the [[Minimal polynomial (field theory)|minimal polynomial]] for {{tmath|\textstyle \varphi^n}} for any non-zero integer {{tmath|n}}.<ref>For {{tmath|1=\textstyle \varphi^0 = 1}}, which is its own conjugate, the polynomial <math>\textstyle x^2 - 2x + 1 = {}\!</math><math>\textstyle (x - 1)^2</math> is not minimal.</ref> The quadratic polynomial {{tmath|1=\textstyle x^2 - 5F_nx + (-1)^{n+1}5 }} is the minimal polynomial for {{tmath|\textstyle \varphi^n\sqrt5 }}.<ref>Because, as described in {{slink||Conjugation and norm}}, <math>\textstyle (x - \alpha)(x - \overline\alpha) = {}\!</math><math>\textstyle x^2 - \mathrm{tr}(\alpha)x + \mathrm{N}(\alpha)</math> for any {{tmath|\alpha}} in {{tmath|\Q(\sqrt5~\!)}}. In this case, {{tmath|1=\textstyle \mathrm{tr}(\varphi^n) = L_n}}, {{tmath|1=\textstyle \mathrm{N}(\varphi^n) = (-1)^n}}, {{tmath|1=\textstyle \mathrm{tr}(\varphi^n\sqrt5~\!) = 5F_n}}, and {{tmath|1=\textstyle \mathrm{N}(\varphi^n\sqrt5~\!) = (-1)^n(-5)}}.</ref>

In the [[Limit of a sequence|limit]], consecutive Fibonacci or Lucas numbers approach a ratio of {{tmath|\varphi}}, and the ratio of Lucas to Fibonacci numbers approaches {{tmath|\sqrt5}}:{{r|A002163}}
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac {F_{n+1}}{F_n} &= \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{L_{n+1}}{L_n} = \varphi,
& \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac {L_n}{F_n} &= \sqrt5.
\end{align}</math>

Theorems about the Fibonacci numbers – for example, [[Fibonacci sequence#Primes and divisibility|divisibility properties]] such as if {{tmath|n}} [[divides]] {{tmath|m}} then {{tmath|F_n}} divides {{tmath|F_m}} – can be conveniently proven using {{Q(√5)}}.<ref>{{harvnb|Dodd|1983|at=§ 9.4 "Divisibility Properties of the Fibonacci Numbers", {{pgs|119–126}} }} proves this and various related results. See also {{harvnb|Carlitz|1964}}.</ref>

== Relation to fivefold symmetry ==
The golden ratio {{tmath|1= \varphi = \tfrac12\bigl(1 + \sqrt5~\!\bigr)}} is the ratio between the lengths of a [[diagonal]] and a side of a [[regular pentagon]], so the golden field and golden integers feature prominently in the metrical geometry of the regular pentagon and its symmetry system, as well as higher-dimensional objects and symmetries involving five-fold symmetry.

=== Euclidean plane ===

[[File:Fifth cyclotomic field and the golden ratio.png |thumb |upright=1.25 |The golden ratio is related to the fifth roots of unity.]]
Let {{tmath|1= \zeta = {\exp}\bigl(2\pi i/5 \bigr) }} be the 5th [[root of unity]], a [[complex number]] of unit absolute value spaced {{tmath|\tfrac15}} of a [[full turn]] from {{tmath|1}} around the [[unit complex numbers|unit circle]], satisfying {{tmath|1=\textstyle \zeta^5 = 1}}. Then the fifth [[cyclotomic field]] {{tmath|\Q(\zeta)}} is the [[field extension]] of the rational numbers formed by [[Adjunction (field theory)|adjoining]] {{tmath|\zeta}} (or equivalently, adjoining any of {{tmath|\textstyle \zeta^2}}, {{tmath|\textstyle \zeta^3}} or {{tmath|\textstyle \zeta^4}}). Elements of {{tmath|\Q(\zeta)}} are numbers of the form <math>\textstyle a_0 + a_1\zeta + {}</math><math>a_2\zeta^2 + {}</math>{{nobr|<math>a_3\zeta^3 + a_4\zeta^4 </math>}}, with rational coefficients. {{tmath|\Q(\zeta)}} is [[quartic function|of degree four]] over the rational numbers: any four of the five roots are [[linear independence|linearly independent]] over {{tmath|\Q}}, but all five sum to zero. However, {{tmath|\Q(\zeta)}} is only [[quadratic function|of degree two]] over {{Q(√5)}},
<math display=block>\begin{align}
x^5 - 1 &= (x - 1)\bigl(x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1\bigr) \\[2mu]
&= (x - 1)\bigl(x^2 + \overline \varphi x + 1\bigr)\bigl(x^2 + \varphi x + 1\bigr) \\[2mu]
&= (x - 1)\bigl(x - \zeta\bigr)\bigl(x - \zeta^4\bigr)\bigl(x - \zeta^2\bigr)\bigl(x - \zeta^3\bigr),
\end{align}</math>
where the [[#Conjugation and norm|conjugate]] {{tmath|1= \overline \varphi = 1 - \varphi}}. The elements of {{tmath|\Q(\zeta)}} can alternately be represented as {{tmath|\alpha + \beta\zeta}}, where {{tmath|\alpha}} and {{tmath|\beta}} are elements of {{Q(√5)}}:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
& a_0 + a_1\zeta + a_2\zeta^2 + a_3\zeta^3 + a_4\zeta^4 \\[3mu]
&\qquad = \bigl(a_0 - a_2 + \overline \varphi a_3 - \overline \varphi a_4\bigr) + \bigl(a_1 - \overline \varphi a_2 + \overline \varphi a_3 - a_4 \bigr)\zeta.
\end{align}</math>

Conversely, {{Q(√5)}} is a [[Subfield (mathematics)|subfield]] of {{tmath|\Q(\zeta)}}. For any primitive root of unity {{tmath|\zeta_n}}, the maximal real subfield of the cyclotomic field {{tmath|\Q(\zeta_n)}} is the field {{tmath|\Q(\zeta_n + \zeta_n^{-1})}}; see [[Minimal polynomial of 2cos(2pi/n)|Minimal polynomial of {{tmath|2\cos(2\pi/n)}}]]. In our case {{tmath|1= n = 5}}, <math>\textstyle (\zeta + \zeta^{-1}{)}^2 + {}</math>{{nobr|<math>(\zeta + \zeta^{-1}) - 1 = 0</math>,}} so {{tmath|1= \zeta + \zeta^{-1} }} is the positive root of the quadratic polynomial {{tmath|\textstyle x^2 + x - 1}}, namely {{tmath|\textstyle \varphi^{-1} }}, and the maximal real subfield of {{tmath|\Q(\zeta)}} is {{Q(√5)}}.<ref>{{harvnb|Shurman|1997|p=77}}. {{pb}} More generally, for any odd prime {{tmath|p}}, the field {{tmath|\textstyle \Q\Bigl(~\!\!\sqrt{(-1)^{(p-1)/2} p}~\!\Bigr)}} is a subfield of {{tmath|\Q(\zeta_p)}}. Moreover, by the [[Kronecker–Weber theorem]], every abelian extension of the rationals is contained in some cyclotomic field. See {{harvnb|Ireland|Rosen|1990|pp=199–200}}.</ref>

[[File:Diagonals of a decagon.png |thumb |upright=1.25 |Diagonals of a unit-circumradius regular decagon are square roots of golden integers.]]
The squared [[Absolute value#Complex numbers|absolute value]] of any element of {{tmath|\Q(\zeta)}} is an element of {{Q(√5)}}:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
|\alpha + \beta\zeta|^2 &= (\alpha + \beta\zeta)(\alpha + \beta\zeta^{-1}) = \alpha^2 + \beta^2 + \alpha\beta\varphi^{-1}.
\end{align}</math>
In particular, the [[squared length]] of the side of a regular pentagon of unit [[circumradius]] is <math>\textstyle |\zeta - 1|{}^2 = {}</math><math>2+\overline\varphi = {}</math><math>\textstyle \varphi^{-1}\sqrt5</math> and the squared length of its diagonal is <math>\textstyle |\zeta^2 - 1|{}^2 = {}</math><math> 2+\varphi = {} </math>{{nobr|<math> \varphi\sqrt5</math>;}} these two numbers are conjugates, associates of {{tmath|\sqrt5}}. In a [[regular decagon]] with unit circumradius, the squared length of a side is <math>\textstyle |\zeta^2 + 1|{}^2 = \varphi^{-2}</math> and the squared length of a diagonal between vertices three apart is {{nobr|<math>\textstyle |\zeta + 1|{}^2 = \textstyle \varphi^2</math>.}}

Golden integers are involved in the [[trigonometric]] study of fivefold symmetries. By the [[quadratic formula]],
<math display=block>\begin{alignat}{3}
\zeta &= \tfrac12\bigl({-\overline\varphi} + {\textstyle \sqrt{\,\overline\varphi{}^2 - 4}}~\!\bigr)
&{}= -\tfrac12\overline\varphi + \tfrac12\sqrt{-2 - \varphi }, \\[6mu]
\zeta^2 &= \tfrac12\bigl({-\varphi} + {\textstyle \sqrt{\varphi{}^2 - 4}}~\!\bigr)
&{}= -\tfrac12\varphi + {\textstyle \tfrac12\sqrt{-2 - \overline\varphi } }.
\end{alignat}</math>

Angles of {{tmath|\tfrac25\pi}} and {{tmath|\tfrac45\pi}} thus have golden rational [[cosine]]s but their [[sine]]s are the square roots of golden rational numbers.<ref>{{harvnb|Bradie|2002}}; {{harvnb|Huntley|1970|pp=39–41}}.</ref>
<math display=block>\begin{align}
\cos\tfrac25\pi &= -\tfrac12\overline\varphi, & \sin\tfrac25\pi &= \tfrac12\sqrt{2+\varphi}, \\[6mu]
\cos\tfrac45\pi &= -\tfrac12\varphi,          & \sin\tfrac45\pi &= \tfrac12{\textstyle \sqrt{2+\overline\varphi}}.
\end{align}</math>

=== Three-dimensional space ===
A [[regular icosahedron]] with edge length {{tmath|2}} can be oriented so that the [[Cartesian coordinate]]s of its vertices are{{sfn|Steeb|Hardy|Tanski|2012|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=UdI7DQAAQBAJ&pg=PA211 211]}}
<math display="block"> \left(0, \pm 1, \pm \varphi \right), \left(\pm 1, \pm \varphi, 0 \right), \left(\pm \varphi, 0, \pm 1 \right). </math>

=== Four-dimensional space ===

The [[600-cell]] is a [[regular 4-polytope]] with 120 vertices, 720 edges, 1200 triangular faces, and 600 tetrahedral cells. It has [[kaleidoscopic symmetry]] {{tmath|[5, 3, 3]}} generated by four mirrors which can be conveniently oriented as {{tmath|1= \sqrt5 x_1 = x_2 + x_3 + x_4}}, {{tmath|1= x_1 = x_2}}, {{tmath|1= x_2 = x_3}}, and {{tmath|1= x_3 = x_4}}. Then the 120 vertices have golden-integer coordinates: arbitrary permutations of {{tmath|\textstyle (\varphi, \varphi, \varphi, \varphi^{-2})}} and {{tmath|\textstyle (\varphi^{-1}, \varphi^{-1}, \varphi^{-1}, \varphi^2)}} with an even number of minus signs, {{tmath|(1, 1, 1, \sqrt5)}} with an odd number of minus signs, and {{tmath|(\pm2, \pm2, 0, 0)}}.<ref>{{harvnb|Coxeter|1985}}; {{harvnb|Denney|Hooker|Johnson|Robinson|2020}}.</ref>

=== Higher dimensions ===

The [[icosian]]s are a special set of [[quaternion]]s that are used in a construction of the [[E8 lattice|E<sub>8</sub> lattice]]. Each component of an icosian always belongs to the golden field.{{sfnm|1a1=Conway|1a2=Sloane|1y=1999|1pp=207–208 |2a1=Pleasants|2y=2002|2pp=213–214}} The icosians of unit norm are the vertices of a 600-cell.{{sfn|Denney|Hooker|Johnson|Robinson|2020}}

== Quasiperiodicity ==
[[File:Fibonacci chain – one-dimensional quasicrystal.png |upright=1.25 |thumb |The Fibonacci chain, a one-dimensional quasicrystal, constructed by the cut-and-project method]]

Golden integers are used in studying [[quasicrystal]]s.{{sfn|Sporn|2021}}

==Other applications==

The quintic case of [[Fermat's Last Theorem]], that there are no nontrivial integer solutions to the equation {{tmath|1=\textstyle a^5 + b^5 = c^5}}, was proved using {{Q(√5)}} by [[Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet]] and [[Adrien-Marie Legendre]] in 1825–1830.<ref>{{harvnb|Ribenboim|1999}}; {{harvnb| Dirichlet|1828}}; {{harvnb|Legendre|1830}}; {{harvnb|Dodd|1983|at=§{{nbsp}}9.3 "The Equation {{tmath|1=\textstyle x^5 + y^5 + z^5 = 0}}", {{pgs|110–118}}. }}</ref>

In [[enumerative geometry]], it is proven that every non-singular [[cubic surface]] contains exactly 27 lines. The [[Clebsch surface]] is unusual in that all 27 lines can be defined over the [[real number]]s.{{sfn|Baez|2016}} They can, in fact, be defined over the golden field.{{sfnm|1a1=Hunt|1y=1996 |2a1=Polo-Blanco|2a2=Top|2y=2009}}

In [[quantum information theory]], an [[abelian extension]] of the golden field is used in a construction of a [[SIC-POVM]] in four-dimensional complex vector space.{{sfnm|1a1=Appleby|1a2=Bengtsson|1a3=Grassl|1a4=Harrison|1y=2022|2a1=Bengtsson|2y=2017}}
